'''''Veronica hederifolia''''', the '''ivy-leaved speedwell''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> is a [[flowering plant]] belonging to the family [[Plantaginaceae]]. It is native to Europe, western Asia and north Africa<ref name=powo>{{cite web |work=Plants of the World Online |title=Veronica hederifolia |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/results?q=veronica%20hederifolia |access-date=8 April 2022 }}</ref> and it is present in other places as an [[introduced species]] and a common [[weed]].  Solitary blue flowers occur in leaf axils, each with a corolla up to {{convert|1|cm|spell=in|1}} wide. The fruit is a [[dehiscent]] [[capsule (botany)|capsule]].

==Description==
It is an annual herb with procumbent to climbing stems up to {{convert|60|cm}} long. The stems are green to purplish, round, with abundant spreading, wavy hairs 1 mm long (but forming a thick line along one side of the stem). The leaves are opposite, becoming alternate higher up the stem, with 4–15 mm long [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] and no stipules. The blades are divided shallowly into 5 lobes, like [[Hedera helix|ivy]], (sometimes 3–7 lobes or entire), darker above than below, up to 1.5 cm long, and are downy above and below with long hairs on the margins.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |publisher=C&M Floristics |location=Suffolk}}</ref>

The flowers are solitary in the leaf axils on pedicels up to 18 mm long. The calyx has four triangular lobes which expand after flowering. There are 4–5 pale lilac petals, 2 mm long, with darker veins. There are 2 stamens, with blue anthers, and one style. The fruits are glabrous, 2-celled (sometimes 1–3) capsules.<ref name="Stace" />

==Taxonomy==
It was named by Linnaeus in [[Species Plantarum]] in 1753. The specific epithet "hederifolia" simply means "ivy-leaved."

There are three subspecies: ''hederifolia'', ''lucorum'' (Klett & Richt.) Hartl and ''insularis'' Gamisans. The latter occurs only in Corsica.<ref name="GBIF" />

==Distribution==
It is thought to be native to southern Europe and widely naturalised outside that range, including in northern Europe as far as [[Scandinavia]], in the [[United States]], [[Japan]], [[Australia]], [[New Zealand]], and scattered places elsewhere.<ref name=GBIF>{{cite web |last1=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |title=Veronica hederifolia L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/3172070 |access-date=13 April 2022}}</ref><ref name=Atlas>{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=C.D. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Dines |first3=T.D. |title=New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |date=2002 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford}}</ref>

In Britain, it is ubiquitous throughout the lowlands, becoming rare only in the mountains of [[Cumbria]] and the [[Highlands and Islands]] of [[Scotland]]. In [[Ireland]] it has a similarly south-easterly distribution, fading out in the west.<ref name="Atlas" />

==Ecology and habitat==
In Britain, it is mainly associated with inhabited areas, being common in towns and villages where it grows in gardens, hedges, road sides and on waste ground. It is also found, less commonly, in arable fields and more wild places. It is a lowland plant; its maximum recorded altitude was {{Convert abbreviated|380|m}} at [[Malham Moor]] in Yorkshire (although that was in 1888, so it might have been an atypical occurrence).<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pearman |first1=D.A. |title=Altitudinal Limits of British Plants, 2021 |url=https://bsbi.org/altitudes}}</ref>
